content: The physical examination of patients often reveals significant findings that are diagnostic or highly suggestive of specific conditions. Below are detailed descriptions of potential findings across various systems: Appearance of the Patient Patients may present with a variety of physical appearances depending on the underlying condition. Vital Signs Patients may exhibit high-grade or low-grade fever. Hypothermia or hyperthermia may be observed. Tachycardia can occur with a regular pulse or an irregularly irregular pulse. Bradycardia may also be present, with either a regular pulse or an irregularly irregular pulse. Tachypnea or bradypnea may be noted. Kussmaul respirations may be present in advanced disease states. Pulses may be weak, bounding, alternating (pulsus alternans), paradoxical, or asymmetric. Blood pressure may be elevated or decreased, with variations in pulse pressure, including normal, wide, or narrow pulse pressure. Skin Cyanosis, indicating hypoxemia, may be present. Jaundice, suggestive of hyperbilirubinemia, may be observed. Pallor, which may indicate anemia or poor perfusion, can be noted. Bruises may be present, potentially indicating trauma or coagulopathy. Skin findings may be further described using dermatological references. HEENT (Head, Eyes, Ears, Nose, and Throat) Abnormalities of the head or hair may be present, including evidence of trauma. Icteric sclera may indicate jaundice. Nystagmus, an involuntary eye movement, may be observed. Extraocular movements may be abnormal, suggesting cranial nerve dysfunction. Pupils may be non-reactive to light, accommodation, or both, indicating potential neurological impairment. Ophthalmoscopic examination may reveal abnormalities such as retinal changes or optic disc swelling. Hearing acuity may be reduced. The Weber test may yield abnormal findings, indicating conductive or sensorineural hearing loss. (Note: An abnormal Weber test is preferred terminology to avoid confusion.) The Rinne test may also be abnormal, indicating conductive hearing loss. (Note: An abnormal Rinne test is preferred terminology to avoid confusion.) These findings, when interpreted in the context of the patient’s clinical presentation, can provide critical diagnostic insights.
